messages.subject: Difficulties to add continuous covariate to the habitat mask
messages.subject_clean: Difficulties to add continuous covariate to the habitat mask
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am calculating lynx densities in a study area in Switzerland using secr and obtained a density of 1.100897e-04 (with model bk).

Now I am trying to add to my habitat mask a covariate of habitat suitability, which is a continuous covariate having values ranging from 44 to 831. The raster I was provided with is for several countries on the European continent. As my study area concerns a small region of Switzerland, I tried in two ways:

First way:

a) Going through QGis I output a text file that gives me for each pixel inside my habitat mask the associated value of the habitat suitability raster.
b) I imported the text file in R

> head(testmask_cov)

       x      y SAMPLE_1

1 554821 125086      595

2 555821 125086      577

3 556821 125086      558

4 557821 125086      551

5 558821 125086      552

6 559821 125086      546

and added the covariate to my mask like this:

> covariates(mask_prox) <- testmask_cov

When I plot it:

> plot(mask_prox, covariate= "SAMPLE_1", dots = F,

     title= "Habitat \n suitability ")

> points(traps_analysis[,"x"], traps_analysis[, "y"], pch=20, bg=grey(1), col='black')

Then I tried to obtain the density~covariate with secr.fit: (I tried with g0~1 and g0~bk , it It gives me the same warning message)

> Mbk_covariate <- secr.fit(lynx_capthist, mask= mask_prox, model = list(D~"SAMPLE_1", g0~bk, sigma~1),

                               details = list(fastproximity = FALSE),

                               method = "none")

Checking data

Preparing detection design matrices

Preparing density design matrix

Finding initial parameter values...

Initial values  D = 1e-04, g0 = 0.12708, sigma = 4652.96228

Computing Hessian with fdHess in nlme

   1   -543.775    -9.2243     0.0000    -1.9270     0.0000     8.4453

…

 22   -543.775    -9.2243     0.0000    -1.9270     0.0000     8.4453

Completed in 22.89 seconds at 10:41:48 01 jui 2022

Message d'avis :

Dans secr.fit(lynx_capthist, mask = mask_prox, model = list(D ~  :

  at least one variance calculation failed
2nd way:
I imported the raster directly into R, and tried to add the covariate with addCovariate:

> str_name <- ‘habitat_suitability.tif'

> imported_raster=raster(str_name)

> addCovariates (mask_prox, imported_raster, columns = NULL, strict = FALSE, replace = FALSE)

[…] #I didn't want to copy the long list

Message d'avis :

Dans addCovariates(mask_prox, imported_raster, columns = NULL, strict = FALSE,  :

  missing values among new covariates

> head(covariates(mask_prox))

NULL

I saw that there is a repair function (« Habitat masks in the package secr » by Murray Efford, 2022-01-06, page 12) and I tried it, but as I don't have a covariate to my mask I think it's normal that it doesn't work... :P

I must admit that this is the first time I am working with covariates and I am a bit lost...

Could someone advise me on how to add this covariate to my mask correctly?

Best regards,

Inès

messages.subject: Re: Difficulties to add continuous covariate to the habitat mask
messages.subject_clean: Difficulties to add continuous covariate to the habitat mask
messages.body_plain:
Hello Inès
I suspect the primary problem is that there are a few missing values in the data. Missing values are not allowed.
Then note:
1. using method = 'none' does not maximise the likelihood and fit the model (it has a specialised use to re-compute variances for a fitted model)
2. you need to assign the result from addCovariates to an object, e.g.
mask_prox2  <- addCovariates (mask_prox, imported_raster)
I hope this helps
Murray

messages.subject: Re: trouble with snail data
messages.body_plain:
Hi Scott,

secr is for spatial capture-recapture, and I think the problem here is because you've only got one polygon so there's no spatial information -- all snails are seen at the same detector.

If that's really the case, rather than a problem with data input, then I think you'd be better off with a non-spatial CMR package (like Rmarked or marked, but I'm not sure what is out there).

Cheers,
Ian

messages.body_plain:
Here's a function that uses functions from package 'sf' to project coordinates in an existing capthist object, assuming initially lat-lon. 'crs' follows convention in 'sf'.

transformCH <- function(capthist, crs, initial = c('latlon', 'lonlat')) {
    if (ms(capthist)) {
        out <- lapply(capthist, transformCH, crs = crs, initial = initial)
        class(out) <- class(capthist)
        out
    }
    else {
        xyorder <- switch(initial, latlon = 2:1, lonlat = 1:2)
        latlon <- sf::st_as_sf(traps(capthist), coords = xyorder)
        sf::st_crs(latlon) <- 4326  # specify initial CRS: WGS84 lat-lon
        traps(capthist)[,] <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(latlon, crs = crs))
        xycoord <- xy(capthist)
        if (!is.null(xycoord)) {
            latlonXY <- sf::st_as_sf(xycoord, coords = xyorder)
            sf::st_crs(latlonXY) <- sf::st_crs(latlon)
            xycoord <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(latlonXY, crs = crs))
            xy(capthist)[,] <- xycoord
        }
        xycoord <- telemetryxy(capthist)
        if (!is.null(xycoord)) {
            latlonXY <- sf::st_as_sf(xycoord, coords = xyorder)
            sf::st_crs(latlonXY) <- sf::st_crs(latlon)
            xycoord <- sf::st_coordinates(sf::st_transform(latlonXY, crs = crs))
            telemetryxy(capthist)[,] <- xycoord
        }
        capthist
    }
}

require('sf')
FF1utm <- transformCH(FF1, crs = 8693, initial = 'latlon')   # EPSG 8693 = UTM 55N
plot(FF1utm, border = 0, tracks = TRUE)

# I would be worried that there are so many long observed movements...

messages.body_plain:
Hello Murray and Ian,

Yes, these are endangered snails on Guam. Don't really understand what project the lat/lon means. I thought I had used degree decimals before in program Density without any problems but memory could be wrong on that. Should use UTM's instead? I will try to work through the code you sent but I have a heck of time with R.

I have run the mark recapture data on program Mark and that works just fine, but cannot get a density by doing that.

I plotted some of these points on google earth and agree, there are some long movements being made here. Because the snails are listed endangered we need a permit to handle them. So, we are using photographs to record individuals (the shells have a striped pattern that is individualistic), so no need for a permit, and we are using the photo ID software called "Hotspotter". messages.subject: Accounting for trapping effort openCR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray
and all,

I’m running
openCR on rock wallaby trapping data that spans several years. I’m trying to
adjust for trapping effort as best as I can and I wanted to see if my current
method and estimates can be improved on.

I’m using
trapping data ranging from 2014 to 2021, and in the earlier years they would commonly
set one trap twice in one night, whereby they set and processed the same trap
in the evening and early morning. This would allow two opportunities for a
wallaby to be trapped at that trap location in that one night.

To model this,
I made two separate traps at the same location (jittered the points so they
were only 1m apart). I would then close that second trap at the location if
they had only set it once that night. In 2021, they would only set traps up
once on the night and so essentially 2021 is approximately half the trapping
effort of those earlier trapping years.

My first
question; is this method the best way to model this trapping scenario?

My second
question; is using ‘single’ as the detector type the best option vs ‘multi’?
I will usually put multi as there are examples of multiple animals (2 max) getting caught in the
same trap in my data, however, I’m not sure if this would influence trapping
effort as I’ve run them both and they appear not to make a difference to my
results.

My third;
is there any other ways to account for this variable trapping effort?

There are concerns that the decrease in estimates in 2021 (figure below using
openCR estimates) is due to trapping effort rather than true abundance. I’ve
also been told that estimates in the last session of your model will naturally
drop? Is this correct?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated.

I’ve also
run a non-spatial CR with the openCR package just to compare the results
(figure below). I’m used to non-spatial models showing lower estimates than spatial
models, however, the pattern observed below is a little all over the place.

Thanks!

Kristen

messages.subject: Re: Accounting for trapping effort openCR
messages.body_plain:
Hello Kristen
I don't pretend to have definitive answers, but here are some thoughts.

1. Your description 'set and processed the same trap in the evening and early morning' seems to describe two distinct capture occasions, rather like the am and pm occasions of the Coulombe house mouse dataset in Otis et al. 1978. I'm assuming the traps were opened for just a few hours at each time to minimize stress on the animals (I once helped briefly with a YFRW study like that). If so then I would think it simpler to just enter the data as occasion-specific, rather than injecting supernumerary traps and turning them off and on (presumably with 'usage'). You might want to consider an occasion-specific covariate am vs pm. But I doubt these fiddles will make a noticeable difference to the estimates.

Your two-trap approach has the problem that 'trapping' implies a maximum of one capture per occasion per animal, whereas a wallaby might be caught both evening and morning, at least in principle.

2. The 'single' option is treated the same as 'multi' in practice, because there is no probability model for the single-catch case (we approximate with 'multi', expecting good density estimates but biased g0-hat or lambda0-hat). For each closed population you can fit a single-catch model with the 'simulation and inverse-prediction' method in the new package 'ipsecr', but that is sort of academic and unnecessary.

3. Other ways - not really. For non-trapping data ('proximity' and 'count' detectors) you can allow for the duration of detector opening in the usage attribute, but that doesn't properly represent what is going on (wallaby caught at most once on each occasion).

Regarding the plot: Jolly-Seber estimates in the last (and first) session of a non-spatial series are strongly biased down by individual heterogeneity - the classic references are by Gilbert and by Carothers from the early 1970s. I guess that might also happen with spatial data when there is unmodelled heterogeneity, but I haven't investigated and would expect a smaller effect. The jump in 2016 also needs explaining.

If you have robust-design data (multiple trapping occasions in each year) then why not add a plot of the closed-population spatial estimates? I am a bit unsure about using open spatial estimates for density, as they may be affected by the choice of model structures for survival and recruitment. Something like fits <- lapply(ch, secr.fit, buffer = 500, etc.) will do it. Then fits <- secrlist(fits); predict(fits)

Cheers
Murray
